translationMethod: Original English translations from the repository's Chinese edition. Stories are concise retellings of that edition, not historical verification. Textual uncertainties are recorded separately.
entries: Zhongli Attains the Way
Heaven and earth open, forming a fortunate bond.
On a fortunate day and at a fitting hour, all things are complete.
To receive this lot is no small matter.
Act with loyalty and integrity, and the emperor will summon you.

Guanyin takes up the brush to give advance notice, though the appointed time of the year has not arrived. The opening phrase is unclear in this edition. The image is Pangu first opening heaven and earth: the traditional reading calls all matters auspicious.

In the legend recorded here, Zhongli Quan, also called Yunfang and Zhengyang, is a Han general. After defeat, a monk leads him to a cave in the Zhongnan Mountains. Reflecting on worldly success and failure, he leaves office and learns the arts of immortality from Donghua Dijun. He later lives in seclusion, is consulted on affairs of state, and becomes the teacher of Lü Dongbin and a leading figure among the Eight Immortals.
Su Qin Fails to Gain Office
The whale, not yet transformed, remains in the rivers.
It cannot yet rise aloft and aspire to greater heights.
On another day its towering form will change.
Then you may leap through the Dragon Gate in a single bound.
Endure where you can; be patient where you must. Wait for the proper time: achievement and office remain possible. The image is a whale not yet transformed; matters call for patience and timing.

Su Qin of Luoyang studies under Guiguzi. His repeated proposals to the ruler of Qin fail, and he returns home penniless to a cold reception from his family. Ashamed, he studies the military text Yinfu with determination, pricking his thigh with an awl to stay awake. He later advocates an alliance of six states against Qin and bears the seals of their chief ministers.
Dong Yong Sells Himself into Servitude
Through wind and rain you make your way home.
Your plight is just like that of a swallow.
It carries mud in its beak to build a nest.
When the nest finally falls, it must gather mud again.
A thousand schemes, ceaseless effort morning and evening: who knew this undertaking would end in such worry? The image is a swallow carrying mud; matters require exhausting effort and care.

Dong Yong loses his mother young and supports his father. Unable to pay for his father's burial, he borrows money and pledges himself to servitude. Heaven, moved by his filial devotion, sends a celestial maiden to help him. She marries him and weaves three hundred lengths of silk to repay the debt, then reveals her identity and returns to heaven. This edition adds that their son later wins first place in the imperial examination.
Yulian Is Reunited with Shipeng
An ancient mirror, broken for a thousand years, becomes whole again.
The woman seeks her husband anew; the man weds again.
From this time the household takes on a renewed appearance.
Further blessings and prosperity come to children and grandchildren.

Gold appears when sand is washed away; one rides a dragon and treads upon a tiger. Although there is worry and toil, something is gained. The image is an old mirror reunited: effort brings valuable help.

In the story of the Thorn Hairpin, the poor scholar Wang Shipeng marries Qian Yulian and travels to the capital for the examinations. Sun Ruquan tries to force Yulian to marry him. She throws herself into a river but is rescued. Shipeng wins first place and refuses a chief minister's daughter. After repeated hardships, the married couple are reunited.
Liu Chen Encounters Immortals
You bore into the earth with an awl, seeking a spring.
The harder you strive, the harder it is to obtain.
Unexpectedly, without intent, you meet an understanding friend.
Together you ascend to the blue heavens, hand in hand.
What you desire may be sought in the west; yet staying where you are may offer a better basis for planning. The image is seeking a spring with an awl: difficulties come first, ease later.

During the Eastern Han, Liu Chen and Ruan Zhao enter Mount Tiantai to gather herbs. They meet two celestial maidens and marry them. After what seems to be half a year, they return home to find that seven generations have passed and nobody knows them. They try to return to the maidens but cannot find the path. The story contrasts deliberate striving with an unexpected encounter.
Rengui Meets His Sovereign
You cast yourself beneath the cliff, where the bronze bird dwells.
This task must fall to a person of true resolve.
Who can gain what is sought through planning and effort?
Such a person is without equal throughout heaven and earth.

There is no surplus for daily use; a simple life accepts poverty. Await the time of benefit and contentment. Parts of this commentary are unclear in the Chinese edition. Its image is a bird beneath a cliff, traditionally read as a favorable sign when one follows the appropriate course.

Xue Rengui joins the army repeatedly but remains a cook, while others claim credit for his victories. When Emperor Taizong is pursued by Gaisu, Rengui rescues him in a moment of danger. The emperor appoints him commander, and he later leads eastern campaigns and wins distinction.
Lady Su Flees Disaster
Hurrying about, you meet obstacles and danger upon danger.
Dragging water and mud, you struggle over the mountains.
Still you hope to seek a livelihood in another land.
Through countless villages and distant miles, you have not returned.

Retreat is possible, but advancing is difficult. Keep to established ways rather than reaching for higher station. The image is trudging through mud and water; maintaining what is established is traditionally favorable.

In this legend set in King Jing's Zhou court, Queen Su Ying can converse with parrots and wins the ruler's admiration. The jealous Mei Yuchun frames her. Another woman suffers punishment in her place, and Su Ying escapes to White Horse Temple, where she gives birth to a prince. The story concerns finding a way to endure adversity.
Pei Du Returns the Jade Belts
Pines and cypresses flourish in the dense woodland.
Rain, snow, wind, and frost can do them no harm.
One day they will suddenly be put to great use.
Achievement makes them pillars fit to support the state.
The road is open; a lifetime brings worthy service. Crops and silk flourish, and the household prospers. The image is pines and cypresses in luxuriant woods: distinction accompanies one's affairs.

Pei Du, later chief minister under Tang Emperor Xianzong, is poor in his youth. At Xiangshan Temple he finds priceless jade belts and seeks out their owner to return them. The tale connects this good deed with his later success in the examinations, high office, and campaigns against Caizhou and Huaixi. He retires to Luoyang in old age.
Kongming Assigns His Generals
Please do not conduct this matter from selfish motives.
It calls instead for open and impartial discussion.
Let a clear heart shine, bright and pure.
Like the radiant moon at the center of the sky.
Keep the heart upright and follow sound principles. Sacred guidance is impartial; matters will become clear. The image is the bright moon overhead, signifying openness and understanding.

Zhuge Liang, courtesy name Kongming, studies in seclusion until Liu Bei visits him three times and appoints him military adviser. When Xiahou Dun attacks, Kongming assigns the troops despite Guan Yu's and Zhang Fei's doubts. Victory at Bowang wins their confidence. He later becomes chief minister and is entrusted with the young successor. This is the narrative of the Three Kingdoms tradition.
Pang Juan Examines the Battle Formation
Priceless jade and treasure lie hidden in the stone.
Yet you keep searching for them far away.
It is like carrying a lamp while looking for fire.
Better put things in order than waste your anxious effort.

When the right connections meet, what cannot be accomplished? Do not let desire run without limit: what is before you is real. The image is seeking fire while carrying a lamp; accomplishment awaits its time.

Sun Bin and Pang Juan study under Guiguzi. Jealous of Sun Bin's greater ability, Pang Juan arranges for his feet to be mutilated. Sun Bin feigns madness, escapes to Qi, and becomes its strategist. Pang Juan recognizes but cannot break his battle formation. Sun Bin then uses a decreasing number of cooking fires to lure him to Maling, where the Chinese account says he is killed by hidden crossbowmen.
The Military Writings Are Entrusted to Jiang Wei
The success you seek would be no ordinary achievement.
Yet family connections are briefly occupied with other matters.
In the end the arrow will reach the deer.
A benefactor will guide you toward those who can help.

A change is contemplated, yet the ending is peaceful. If you ask how to proceed, remain close to a helpful person. The image is good fortune emerging from misfortune; undertakings are traditionally favorable.

Jiang Wei begins as a Wei officer but is won over by Kongming, who values his courage and intelligence. During his final illness on the northern campaigns, Kongming entrusts Jiang Wei with twenty-four chapters of military writings, described here as 104,112 characters. He hopes Jiang Wei will carry on his unfinished purpose.
Wu Ji Meets His Teacher
Adversity gives way to peace within a short distance.
For now, meet the worthy person coming from the mountain.
When tiger and rabbit bring favorable news,
Resolve makes a busy undertaking turn to ease.

Hemp is exchanged for silk; the following phrase about striking both feet is obscure in this edition. Seek clarity: misfortune can give rise to good fortune. The image is blessing within trouble, with difficulty preceding improvement.

The woodcutter Wu Ji laughs at Jiang Ziya fishing with a straight hook. Jiang predicts that he will kill someone that day; Wu Ji then accidentally causes a man's death while carrying firewood. Temporarily released to care for his mother, he seeks Jiang's help. Jiang teaches him military arts and, in the legend, evades the divination that would reveal him. Wu Ji later introduces King Wen to Jiang and becomes a general.
Luo Tong Is Appointed Commander
From childhood you were born into wealth and honor.
Everything before your eyes was splendid and luxurious.
The ruler grants you purple robes and a jeweled belt.
Your reputation may be acclaimed throughout the world.

A prisoner meets a pardon; the sick find peace. At the Dragon Gate comes recognition, and fame reaches the imperial capital. The image is an encounter at the Dragon Gate: change is traditionally highly auspicious.

In this early Tang legend, seventeen-year-old Luo Tong wins the commander's seal in a martial contest and leads a northern campaign. He later angers Emperor Taizong and loses office. Cheng Yaojin intercedes and obtains his pardon. The episode represents achievement at a young age.
Ziya Leaves Office
You are like an immortal crane leaving its cage.
Freed from the cage, every road opens.
North, south, east, and west present no barriers.
You may soar straight toward the palace in the ninth heaven.
Move freely without anxiety; the roads are open. Follow your inclination in untroubled freedom. The image is a crane released from a cage, with difficulty preceding good fortune.

In Investiture of the Gods, Jiang Ziya reaches seventy-two without worldly success. He receives an astronomical office after exposing a pipa spirit, but fails to dissuade King Zhou from building the extravagant Deer Terrace. He leaves the capital for Xiqi. His wife refuses to accompany him, so they separate. He fishes in the Wei River while waiting for his opportunity.
Su Qin Achieves His Ambition
The traveler grieves through the day, unable to swallow his anger.
If sudden disaster appears, do not approach it.
A bird whose woodland nest is broken has nowhere to rest.
Seek a sheltered place where you can settle safely.

When resentment divides people, when can one find redress? Good words go unheeded; keep to established ways and await the time. The image is birds leaving the woods; the commentary anticipates eventual fulfillment.

Su Qin's proposals fail at the Qin court, and he returns home exhausted and penniless. His wife continues weaving and his sister-in-law will not cook for him. He studies the Yinfu text with renewed determination, using an awl to keep himself awake. On returning to public affairs, he persuades six states to unite against Qin and receives their ministerial seals.
Ye Mengxiong Appears Before the Emperor
The furrowed brow and troubled thoughts relax for a time.
An opening in the clouds brings joy of itself.
It is like jade lying hidden in the dirt.
A skilled judge recommends it and lifts it from the dust.

What is gained is not lost; even loss contains benefit. The petty meet adversity while the upright fare well. The image is harmony between yin and yang; planned undertakings are traditionally favorable.

Ye Mengxiong, a successful candidate in the Ming examinations under Jiajing, is described as courageous and loyal. During the Wanli reign, rebellion troubles a frontier region and other generals hesitate. Ye appears before Emperor Shenzong to request command of a punitive expedition in service of the state.
Speaking of Plums to Quench Thirst
Do not heed idle talk of right and wrong.
Morning and evening, it is better to recite Amitabha's name.
If you take wild talk to be the truth,
How can a painted cake satisfy hunger?
With an unsettled heart, reading scriptures is in vain. Like eating a painted cake, it provides no nourishment. The image is trying to satisfy hunger with a picture: appearance outweighs substance.

Cao Cao's soldiers are thirsty and short of water. He tells them that a plum grove lies ahead, where they can eat fruit to quench their thirst. The thought makes their mouths water and briefly eases their thirst. The traditional expression is imagining plums to quench thirst; this lot pairs it with the image of a painted cake.
Cao Guojiu Becomes an Immortal
The golden crow sets in the west; the rabbit rises in the east.
Day and night have followed this cycle from antiquity to now.
Monks and Daoists who understand it find no disadvantage.
Scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants each follow their calling.
With no trouble in the heart, one's work bears fruit, like an arrow released into the sky. The image is the waxing and waning of yin and yang; affairs follow their course.

Cao Guojiu, one of the Eight Immortals, is described here as a Song empress dowager's younger brother who once disregards the law. Ashamed, he gives away his wealth to the poor and cultivates the Way in the Zhongnan Mountains. Zhongli Quan and Lü Dongbin guide him into the ranks of the immortals. This edition identifies him by a jade flute.
Ziyi Is Enfeoffed as Prince
You launch the homebound boat at the head of the rapids.
What purpose is served by stirring wind and waves?
If you seek safety and a steady passage,
Wait for the waves to settle before crossing the danger.

A boat enters swift water: await the right moment in danger. The commentary also says undertakings can be carried out. Its governing image is a boat at dangerous rapids: maintain your position and wait.

Guo Ziyi is a Tang general celebrated for suppressing the rebellions of An Lushan and Shi Siming. Emperor Suzong appoints him supreme commander and Prince of Fenyang. The tale describes him putting on armor again at eighty when enemies threaten, and dying peacefully from illness at eighty-five.
Jiang Taigong Meets King Wen
After long spring rains, the first clear weather brings delight.
The jade rabbit and golden crow grow brighter little by little.
Old affairs disperse, and new undertakings prosper.
Soon, in a single leap, you pass the Dragon Gate.

Under divine protection there is trouble but no lasting danger. The journey is peaceful and ends in an honored return. The image is clearing weather after prolonged rain: affairs accord with one's wishes.

Jiang Shang, known as Ziya, Lü Wang, and Feixiong, withdraws from King Zhou's disorder. At Panxi on the Wei River he fishes with a straight hook: his purpose is to serve a worthy ruler rather than catch fish. King Wen hears of his ability and recruits him as teacher and minister at eighty. He helps Zhou overthrow Shang; King Wu honors him as Shangfu.
Li Dan's Dragon-and-Phoenix Marriage
The union of yin and yang rests with heaven.
Woman and man marry, rejoicing together.
When dragon and snake come into accord,
A gentle dream brings the happiness of reunion.

Plans accord with the heart; marriage is harmonious, a son is foretold, wealth increases, and farming and silkworm raising benefit. The image is the union of yin and yang: harmonious affairs are highly auspicious in the traditional reading.

The folk tale identifies Li Dan as Tang Emperor Ruizong. After Wu Zetian takes power, he is said to live among common people and meet Hu Fengjiao, whom he marries. Each carries half of a square seal given at birth; the matching halves confirm their bond. The dragon represents Li Dan, and the story presents marriage as an affinity ordained by heaven.
The Sixth Yang Son Is Rescued
In drought the fields have withered dry.
Thanks to heaven, sweet rain falls in abundance.
Flowers, fruit trees, grasses, and woods are all refreshed.
Only then is one rainfall known to be worth a thousand gold pieces.
Crops and silk mature abundantly; fortune gradually arrives. Illness meets suitable medicine and the traveler returns. The image is welcome rain in drought: help comes amid difficulty.

Yang Yanzhao is the sixth son of Yang Ye. In the Yang-family legend, enemy forces surround the army. Yang Ye dies at Li Ling's stele and the seventh son is killed while seeking reinforcements. The sixth retreats to Gourd Valley, where a monk from Mount Wutai, identified as his fifth brother, rescues him. The episode is likened to timely rain.
Huaide Marries a Princess
You wish to grasp the immortal cassia in the moon palace.
Why fear that heaven's gate will refuse you entry?
Suddenly, welcome news arrives.
Everyone laughs with joy, wearing the flowers of honor.

Trade brings benefit, though going forward or withdrawing may carry danger. Illness finds peace and litigation proceeds favorably. The image is grasping the moon's cassia: a helpful person assists one's affairs.

Gao Huaide supports Zhao Kuangyin during the Chenqiao coup and becomes a founding general of the Song. He marries the emperor's younger sister, Princess of Yan, and receives the rank of imperial son-in-law. This edition also places him on campaigns against Liao with the Yang generals.
Yin Jiao Meets His Teacher
Reasoning fails, and the household cannot be established.
The fickle, deluded person is like a fallen blossom.
If you ask for a ruler's favor, effort is needed.
Only in the end do you see affairs tangled like hemp.
Avoid disputes; examine matters carefully. An upright heart and sound reasons avert danger. The image is a deluded person on a blocked road: maintain what is established and wait.

In Investiture of the Gods, Yin Jiao, son of Shang's King Zhou, studies under Guangchengzi. Before leaving, he vows to aid Zhou's opponents rather than support his father's wrongdoing. Persuaded otherwise on the way, he breaks that oath and fights his teacher. Jiang Ziya and Randeng trap him between mountains, and Guangchengzi kills him, fulfilling the terms of his vow.
Li Guang's Resourceful Escape
You have passed through repeated worry and danger.
From now on, establish yourself anew without empty effort.
A calmer heart finds a way to put itself at ease.
Meeting a person of ability, you accomplish great deeds.
Litigation eventually finds justification and illness finds safety. In travel and enterprise, an old well meets a fresh spring. This image signifies accomplishment through a benefactor.

The Han general Li Guang is wounded and captured after his troops scatter in battle with the Xiongnu. Pretending to be dead while carried between horses, he suddenly mounts an escort's horse, seizes a bow, and escapes south, shooting at pursuers. Although he survives, he is condemned for the defeat and pays to redeem his sentence. He later returns to service as governor of Youbeiping.
Zhong Kui Attains Understanding
Reports from above and below grow ever less substantial.
From the edge of heaven a letter reaches you.
The letter promises success and distinction.
Yet even at the end, the promise remains empty.

Those above and below are troubled; sought-for leisure does not come. If you aspire to distinction, keeping your present position brings peace. The image is empty reputation: much appearance and little substance.

Zhong Kui wins first place in the examinations but is rejected for his frightening appearance. He attacks the minister who supports the rejection and then kills himself. Granted office as an exorcising deity, he goes to the underworld. Its ruler teaches that a righteous ghost may be divine, while a crooked-hearted person is already a demon. Enlightened, Zhong Kui returns to the human world to subdue evil.
Liu Ji Admonishes His Ruler
Each plan and action calls for another written deliberation.
Looking ahead and behind, you hesitate to act.
When the time arrives, a benefactor lends strength.
Like a mountain or a standing wall, you can then dwell securely.
The old becomes new, as winter flowers meet spring. Earlier obstructions give way to satisfaction. The image is a house with sound walls: steadiness without danger.

Liu Ji, courtesy name Bowen, serves Zhu Yuanzhang as strategist. When allied forces at Anfeng are besieged by Zhang Shicheng, Zhu plans to lead a rescue himself. Liu urgently warns that it will end badly. According to this tale, Zhu is indeed trapped and escapes only with the help of Xu Da and Chang Yuchun.
Consort Li Seeks Judge Bao
The moon rises beautifully in the eastern sky.
In an instant, clouds cover it, though its light remains hidden.
At times it is full, at other times it wanes.
Those who speak against it offer only idle words.
Passing clouds cover the moon; do not remain bewildered. Wait for the clouds to disperse and the result will become visible. The image is a clouded moon: affairs remain obscure and undecided.

In the folk legend, Consort Liu and Guo Huai replace Consort Li's newborn prince with a skinned civet cat. Li is imprisoned, escapes, and survives by begging; grief leaves her blind. Judge Bao investigates, interrogates Guo Huai, and finds Li, bringing the hidden truth to light.
Zhao Zilong Rescues Adou
The precious sword shines as it leaves its case.
While inside, it remained untouched by dust.
Now a benefactor carries it into view.
Its power and authority command everyone's respect.
A treasured sword leaves its case, its brilliance reaching far. A benefactor's guidance makes its worth visible. The image signifies power and authority.

Zhao Yun, courtesy name Zilong, serves Liu Bei. After Cao Cao's forces scatter Liu Bei's family, Zhao finds Lady Mi with the infant Adou beside a ruined wall. She entrusts the child to him and, in the novel's account, dies in a well. Zhao buries her, fights through the encirclement carrying Adou, and reaches Zhang Fei's protection at Changban.
The Gathering at Chessboard Mountain
I urge you not to seek help elsewhere.
A crane flies into the path of a hidden arrow.
If you go to gather firewood, a snake waits in the grass.
Fear of its venomous bite brings further worry.
Keep your counsel and do not meddle in others' affairs. A guilty intention eventually harms its owner. The image is keeping to one's proper place: proceed with vigilance.

In a Tang adventure legend, Xue Rengui is besieged on a western campaign. His son Xue Dingshan and their companions set out to rescue him. At Chessboard Mountain, Dou Yihu's attempt to seize their provisions fails, while his sister Dou Xiantong captures Dingshan. Cheng Yaojin arranges marriages between the two pairs of siblings. Former enemies unite and continue the rescue.
Foyin Meets Su Dongpo
Sit in a quiet place, at ease and free of worry.
After eating, drink tea; sit or lie down as you please.
Let body and mind rest, without haste.
Then grudges and misfortune will not be invited in.
Remaining with established ways brings peace. Ask the immortals, but wait for the time: events may arrive unexpectedly. The image is quiet security, with good fortune dependent on timing.

This literary tale calls Foyin a scholar named Xie Duanqing. Disguised as a temple attendant with Su Dongpo's help, he attracts the emperor's attention and is unexpectedly made a monk. Dongpo later tries to entice him back to secular life, but Foyin resists and instead teaches Dongpo Buddhist principles. The story warns against needless interference and hurried action.
Liu Bei Seeks a Worthy Adviser
The road ahead is distant and dim: do not settle into doubt.
Who knows the jade concealed within the stone?
One day a skilled craftsperson cuts it open clearly.
Only then is the promised fine jade revealed.
Treasure lies in stone, known to few. Wait until its nature is clear, then act. The image is cutting stone to reveal jade; effort brings accomplishment.

Zhuge Liang lives quietly at Longzhong, studying strategy, astronomy, and divination without seeking office. Xu Shu recommends him to Liu Bei, who visits the thatched cottage three times with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei. Zhuge accepts appointment as adviser, later becomes chief minister, and is entrusted with Liu Bei's heir. The episode concerns talent recognized at the proper time.
Yaojin Recruits Rengui
Priceless treasures lie hidden within.
If jade is already there, why seek it outside?
Better wait for a discerning person to recognize it.
Set your heart at ease, then ease it further still.
Gold and jade lie within; why seek elsewhere? A benefactor's guidance removes the need for anxious effort. The image is seeking outside for jade already hidden at home: wait for the time.

Xue Rengui is resting on a mountain when he sees Cheng Yaojin pursued by a tiger. He kills the tiger and saves Cheng, who gives him a command arrow and tells him to join the army. Rengui later becomes a celebrated Tang general. The story links unrecognized ability with eventual recognition.
The Oath in the Peach Garden
In public or private, at home or abroad, act with courtesy and respect.
Speak with loyalty and goodness; be discerning in what you trust.
If the heart is not yet clear, remain still until it settles.
The bright red sun stands directly overhead.
Let the heart be untroubled, clear as autumn water. There is no need for doubt; the matter comes to completion naturally. The image is the sun shining overhead: affairs accord with one's wishes.

Amid the turmoil of the late Han, Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei discover a shared purpose. In Zhang Fei's peach garden they swear brotherhood, with Liu as eldest, Guan second, and Zhang youngest. Their oath calls for mutual aid, relief of distress, service to the state, and protection of ordinary people. They later seek Zhuge Liang's help in restoring the Han.
The Tang Monk Seeks the Scriptures
Put your cap and robes in order and restore the old household ways.
What seemed without end may yet bear fruit.
Sweep the thorns and brambles from the road.
Three people deliberate and come into harmony again.
Do not be anxious or doubtful: a favorable time lies ahead. If you ask about the future, the road is suitable. The image is putting one's dress in order: difficulty first, ease later.

Xuanzang, born Chen Yi, becomes a monk at thirteen and travels to India to obtain Buddhist scriptures. After years of hardship he reaches his destination, studies for fifteen years according to this account, and returns with many scriptures to translate into Chinese. Journey to the West transforms his pilgrimage into a legendary adventure.
Xiangzi Meets Dongbin
Do not worry over the illness or lawsuit before you.
Resources lie throughout the land to be sought.
Like a monkey released from its golden chain,
You return to the mountain cave and roam freely.
Once released from entanglement, let the heart relax. Wait for the proper time to find the right road. The image is a monkey escaping its chain: hardship precedes ease.

Han Xiangzi and Lü Dongbin are members of the Eight Immortals. This edition describes Xiangzi as Han Yu's nephew, a poet fond of wine who studies the Way from youth. Dongbin guides him into the mountains to cultivate and attain immortality. The account gives him a flower basket as emblem and the title Yaohua Dijun.
Li Jing Returns to the Mountains
If you await a time of safety and good fortune,
A candle in the wind is an unsuitable place to stay.
Better gather your things and sit within the inner hall.
There the flame need not flicker; in stillness it shines.
Settle in a quiet place and await the time. Movement invites trouble; maintaining the present course removes doubt. The image is a candle shaken by wind: constancy is favorable.

Li Jing, the Pagoda-Bearing Heavenly King in Investiture of the Gods, helps Jiang Ziya overthrow Shang with his son Nezha. After Zhou is established, he declines worldly rewards and returns to the mountains to cultivate the Way. The account says seven members of the family become sages. Its lesson contrasts pursuit of fame with spiritual cultivation.
He Wenxiu Encounters Misfortune
Moonlight falls upon the heavenly writing in quiet expectation.
Suddenly clouds and mist return, and all grows dim.
Set your heart at ease and wait for the clouds to scatter.
Then make a change and put your plans into practice.

The household faces anxiety and people face trouble; prayers seek protection, though financial loss is still feared. The image is mist covering the moon: desires remain unfulfilled, so keep to established ways.

The poor scholar He Wenxiu's recitation moves Wang Qiongzhen, a wealthy family's daughter, who accompanies him on the flute. They fall in love and flee to Haining. He is falsely imprisoned; she cuts her hair, disguises herself, and endures many hardships. In the Jade Hairpin story they are eventually united.
Meng Jiangnü Searches for Her Husband
News from the distant horizon is hard to fathom.
Do not burden your heart with insistent demands.
If you grind a stone in hope of making a mirror,
Will you not discover that your effort was in vain?
A thousand schemes waste effort. Better remain with established ways than pursue a purpose without foundation. The image is calm constancy: keeping one's proper course is favorable.

Meng Jiangnü's newly married husband is conscripted to build the Great Wall. When she reaches him, she learns that he has died. In the legend, supernatural help reveals his bones, which she identifies with blood from her bitten finger. Her lament causes the wall to collapse. This is a traditional tale of grief and fidelity, not a historical account.
Wu Zetian Takes the Throne
The red sun sets in the west; the rabbit rises in the east.
Yin grows and yang declines, while all affairs pause.
For a woman there is scope to put ability to use.
Added wealth and blessings gladden her heart.
The traditional commentary favors women rather than men. In undertakings, adversity precedes good fortune. The image is yin increasing as yang diminishes: difficulty gives way to ease.

Wu Zetian begins as a consort of Tang Emperor Taizong and later becomes Emperor Gaozong's empress. After Gaozong's death she governs at court, then proclaims herself emperor and changes the dynastic name to Zhou. This edition describes fifteen years of rule, notable achievements, harsh methods, and abdication at an advanced age.
Dong Zhuo Adopts Lü Bu
Remember the many good words you have been given.
Yet you mistake a thief for a son.
Do not covet a little sweetness before your eyes.
Think also of the bitterness it may bring in later years.
Do not make this single mistaken move. Keep the warning in mind and avoid later distress. The image is adopting a thief as one's son: distinguish what is genuine from what is false.

In Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Dong Zhuo wins Lü Bu with a fine horse and money and adopts him as a son. Their relationship deteriorates over Diaochan. Lü Bu joins Wang Yun's plot to kill Dong Zhuo, then urges the destruction of Dong's followers. Later Cao Cao defeats, captures, and executes Lü Bu.
Mulian Rescues His Mother
The sovereign and sacred queen bestow their favor.
Prayers and rites preserve that benefit without diminishing it.
All sentient beings may share in it.
In the human realm and heaven, the hoped-for flourishing arrives.
Do not forget the grace bestowed from heaven. Morning and evening, honor the Buddha and offer incense. The image is heavenly favor descending; accomplishment is traditionally highly auspicious.

Mulian, a Buddhist disciple with supernatural powers, finds his mother suffering as a hungry ghost after her wrongdoing. He asks the Buddha how to save her and is instructed to make Ullambana offerings to monks of the ten directions. Following these instructions, he liberates his mother and helps other parents as well. The tale is associated with the festival on the fifteenth day of the seventh lunar month.
The Pilgrim Attains the Way
Heaven and earth transform, bringing all things to completion.
Through your own work and sustenance, you live in peace.
The countless forms of creation shine in their splendor.
As affairs accord with the heart, give thanks to the sages.

Heaven brings forth all things; plans find an open way. Virtue lends assistance and auspicious signs arrive. The image is harmony between heaven and earth: the traditional reading calls all matters favorable and free of danger.

In Journey to the West, the Monkey King seeks immortality and studies under Patriarch Subhuti, who names him Sun Wukong. After seven years, three knocks on his head and a gesture behind the back tell him to come to the rear door at the third watch. There he learns the Way of longevity, then the seventy-two transformations, before returning to Flower-Fruit Mountain.
Jiang Wei and Deng Ai Contest Their Formations
At chess you meet a worthy opponent: choose each move well.
On the board, black and white remain undecided.
A single move may determine victory or defeat.
You must consider carefully what course is fitting.
What you hope to achieve resembles a game of go. Success at the end calls for thoughtful strategy. The image is meeting one's match at chess: careful planning is favorable.

In this Three Kingdoms tale, Jiang Wei of Shu and Deng Ai of Wei face each other at Qishan. Both deploy Eight Trigrams formations. Jiang then uses a Long Snake formation to trap Deng, who is rescued by Sima Wang. The episode likens worldly affairs to chess, where one mistaken move matters.
Emperor Renzong Recognizes His Mother
Gentleness has long overcome brute strength.
A household that accumulates goodness prospers greatly.
For the person who receives this lot,
It is like finding fine nectar when parched with thirst.
Heaven and earth respond in remarkable ways. Remember the protection attributed to buddhas and deities. The image is goodness and gentleness, with helpful people and harmony in one's affairs.

The civet-cat substitution tale separates the infant future emperor Renzong from his mother, Consort Li. After imprisonment and hardship, she survives as a blind beggar. Judge Bao uncovers the deception by Consort Liu and Guo Huai. With Prince Eight's help, Renzong visits his mother in her humble shelter and brings her back. In the legend, his daily prayers are followed by the restoration of her sight.
Fishing in the Wei River
I urge you to endure and keep your established livelihood.
Steady your heart and do not turn to wrongdoing.
Wait until someone lends a little strength.
Then even an old tree's withered boughs may flower again.
Keep to what is established, and the affair finds completion. Movement brings trouble; quiet brings no blame. The image is dead wood flowering: accomplishment has its own time.

Jiang Shang, also called Ziya and Lü Wang, withdraws from King Zhou's disorder and fishes with a straight hook at Panxi on the Wei River. He is waiting for a ruler who can use his abilities rather than seeking fish. King Wen recruits him at eighty. He helps establish Zhou, is honored by King Wu, and becomes associated with the founding of Qi. The episode illustrates waiting for the right opportunity.
Liang Hao Succeeds in the Examinations
Flowers added to brocade make its colors brighter still.
When fortune arrives, office and advancement bring double joy.
Do not resent that recognition comes late.
One examination triumph carries your name throughout the land.

The established order becomes new; when fortune arrives, achievement follows. A lifelong aim is fulfilled, which the commentary attributes to destiny. The image is flowers added to brocade: great traditional good fortune.

This popular account calls Liang Hao a Song scholar from Shandong, courtesy name Taisu. It describes early examination success followed by repeated unsuccessful attempts, before winning first place in old age. The story celebrates late achievement. Its chronology and reported age differ from historical accounts.
Han Xin Is Appointed Supreme Commander
When autumn comes, the kun bird transforms into the great peng.
It delights in roaming and rising into flight.
Through the clouds it soars for ten thousand miles.
No other bird can equal it.

The kun becomes the peng, beyond the reach of other birds. Plucking the cassia branch adds blessing and office. The image is the kun-peng's transformation: change is highly favorable in the traditional reading.

When Han Xin leaves Liu Bang's service with other departing soldiers, Xiao He pursues him through the night and brings him back. Liu Bang asks why Xiao pursued this man alone. Xiao replies that if the king intends to contest the realm with Chu, only Han Xin can serve as supreme commander. Appointed, Han leads campaigns that help establish Han and is initially made King of Chu.
Wang Xiang Seeks Carp
Heaven and earth are cold, and water turns to ice.
Why grasp so greedily at rank and fame?
Better keep your proper place and sit in quiet.
When time brings a change, clarity comes of itself.
Water freezes into ice; ice melts back into water. Plans and undertakings follow the same pattern. The image is frozen water: anxious striving is unnecessary.

Wang Xiang, a model of filial devotion in the Twenty-Four Filial Exemplars, serves his stepmother respectfully. When she wants fresh fish during freezing weather, he lies bare-bodied on the ice. In the legend it melts, revealing two carp, which he takes home. He later rises to high office. The story attributes the response to his filial sincerity.
Tao Zhugong Returns to the Five Lakes
Across the five lakes and four seas, you may travel freely.
Hoist the sail high and steer at ease.
When a favorable wind comes, you reach your destination.
A boat full of treasures brings joy upon joy.
Rest freely without forcing matters. Wealth and emoluments accumulate, bringing delight. The image is sailing with the wind: the traditional reading calls all affairs smoothly favorable.

Fan Li helps King Goujian of Yue recover from defeat by Wu and ultimately conquer it. Knowing the king can share hardship but not prosperity, he resigns after success and sails away across the lakes. Settling at Tao, he becomes wealthy through business and is known as Tao Zhugong. The story describes several moves and leaves his final whereabouts unknown.
Kongming Enters Sichuan
In summer's fierce heat, the days are longest.
Everyone is distressed by the stifling warmth.
Heaven and earth also understand human wishes.
A gentle southern breeze brings coolness of itself.

Do not remain doubtful about advancing or retreating: an appropriate time will come. In plans and expenditure, avoid reckless action. The image is people troubled by heat; affairs follow a natural course.

Liu Bei lacks a secure territory. Liu Zhang of Yizhou, threatened by Zhang Lu, invites his kinsman Liu Bei to help. In this account Kongming accompanies him, surveys the region's defensible terrain, and makes arrangements that turn western Sichuan into Liu Bei's base.
Li Bai Tries to Scoop Up the Moon
Trying to scoop the moon from water wastes your effort.
After all that labor, there is still nothing.
Do not indulge in idle and confused talk.
Straining heart and strength in vain leaves you alone.
Words are hard to fathom; effort brings weariness and worry. There is anxiety at home while a benefactor is awaited. The image is grasping desire and futile labor.

The poet Li Bai, also known as Taibai and the Banished Immortal, loves wine. In this legend he sees the moon reflected in water while drunk, tries to embrace it, and drowns. A further legendary ending has a white-robed immortal ride a whale to the moon palace. This is a literary tale, not an established account of his death.
Liu Bei Marries in Eastern Wu
The hour of disappointment turns into one of satisfaction.
The dragon's call and tiger's roar sound in accord.
In the blue sky there is a road to the highest heavens.
My hope of achievement has a time to come again.
Go when directed to go; remain when directed to remain. An open way and eventual benefit follow. The image is dragon and tiger calling in harmony: affairs show grounds for hope.

After Liu Bei's wife dies, Sun Quan offers his sister in marriage as a means of detaining Liu Bei and reclaiming Jingzhou. Kongming foresees the plot and gives Zhao Yun sealed instructions to protect him. In Romance of the Three Kingdoms, the pretended marriage becomes real, and Liu Bei returns with Lady Sun, frustrating Zhou Yu's scheme.
Ma Chao Pursues Cao Cao
Treasure found in a dream vanishes when you wake.
You think the southern mountain is only ground to hoe.
If you ask about marriage or illness,
Seek another path on which to find support.
An object in water and its long or short reflection have their allotted form; discussion does not alter them. The image is treasure obtained in a dream: effort is spent in vain.

In the Three Kingdoms story, Ma Chao attacks Cao Cao to avenge his father. Defeated, Cao removes his fine robe and cuts his beard to avoid recognition as he flees on horseback. Cao Hong rescues him, allowing him to survive.
King Wu of Zhou Takes the Throne
A worthy father passes things to his son, and the son to his grandson.
Abundant food and clothing are attributed to heaven.
In the hall, father and mother live in happiness.
Eat when hungry, drink when thirsty, and sleep when tired.

Bamboo pipes channel a spring whose flow continues without interruption. The upright person's plans bring delight. The image is channeling spring water through bamboo: undertakings are traditionally favorable.

King Wu leads the lords against Shang. The defending army turns, and King Zhou dies by fire. Wu takes the throne, distributes stored wealth and grain, releases prisoners and palace women, and honors those wronged by the old regime. He ends warfare and promotes civil order, turning horses and cattle out to pasture. The tale presents the establishment of peaceful government.
An Lushan Rebels
In a shallow, stony stream the running water sounds loudly.
Amid clear wind and bright moon, the helpful person is busy.
Ask which direction the road should take.
Do not pluck the fragrant flowers and grasses of the woods.

Plans and undertakings demand exhausting effort. Keep to established ways and await the time; the commentary calls this favorable. The image is a boat negotiating shallows, with help from a benefactor.

An Lushan, described here as a frontier commander of non-Han origin, gains influence under Emperor Xuanzong and favors from Yang Guifei. Hostility with Yang Guozhong precedes his rebellion. He captures Luoyang and Tong Pass and proclaims Yan, while the emperor flees toward Sichuan. The account ends with An's killing by his own son.
Dong Zhong Seeks His Mother
Let talk of right and wrong pass like wind by your ears.
Fine clothing and ample livelihood come naturally.
Do not dwell on the affairs of former years.
Your intention now accords with mine.
Plans and hopes bring great delight. Work openly and fairly, like a child meeting its mother. The image is a child's reunion with its mother: a benefactor brings favorable prospects.

Dong Zhong is the legendary son of Dong Yong and a celestial maiden. Having learned magical arts and flight, he longs to find his mother. He searches Mount Taibai, where celestial maidens appear on the seventh day of the seventh lunar month, and finally meets her. The associated marriage story appears in lot 3.
King Wen Consults Divination
Remember the frank words spoken to you.
Do not seek another occupation in a foreign place.
Keep firmly to your own established livelihood.
Other courses offer no benefit.
Remain where you can and hold what can be held. Do not take up other affairs; maintain established ways. The image is constancy while awaiting the time.

King Wen divines that a summons from King Zhou will bring seven years of misfortune. He instructs his eldest son to govern Qi by established rules and not leave. Wen is detained at Youli; in this legend his son goes to rescue him and is killed. During confinement, Wen works on the Changes, becoming one of its traditionally credited contributors.
Zhang Liang Withdraws to the Mountains
Climb straight to the high tower to conceal yourself.
Thorns and brambles encircle it like a forest.
Heaven is high; the span of your life lies beyond your sight.
Gaining one thing may instead cost two people.
As if drinking in a drunken state, remain with established ways. Wait for the time and avoid calamity or blame. The image is holding one's position in accordance with circumstances.

Zhang Liang, courtesy name Zifang, helps Liu Bang defeat Xiang Yu and found Han. In this traditional account he perceives that a ruler who shared hardship may kill meritorious supporters after victory. He therefore withdraws from public affairs to preserve his life. Legend says he wanders the mountains with the immortal Chisongzi.
The Battle of Red Cliffs
Carrying firewood to fight a fire makes everything burn.
Even across a vast expanse, the burning continues.
If you ask about honor, prosperity, or setting out,
Better put things in order than waste your anxious effort.

A thousand schemes are less useful than refraining from action. Once entangled, you may bring disaster upon yourself. The image is feeding a fire while trying to extinguish it: guard your conduct carefully.

Cao Cao brings his army to Red Cliffs. Sun Quan's commander Zhou Yu allies with Liu Bei against him. In the novel's telling, Kongming calls up the east wind and Huang Gai sets the linked ships alight. Battle turns the riverfront into a sea of fire and Cao's forces suffer a great defeat.
Su Xiaomei Challenges Her Husband
By day recite poems; beneath the moon sing songs.
Take part in the occasion's play with laughter.
When this meeting comes, it cannot be hidden or avoided.
Together sing congratulations for the wedding bond.
A fair companion is in the house; poems and songs fill it with joy. Good and ill fortune are attributed to one's lot. The governing image counsels constancy and attention to timing.

Su Xiaomei, the legendary gifted sister of Su Dongpo, sets three literary challenges for her bridegroom Qin Shaoyou on their wedding night. He struggles with the third until Dongpo secretly helps him, allowing him to enter the bridal chamber. The tale celebrates literary wit; its characters' relationships belong to popular tradition.
The Tang Monk Attains Awakening
Morning and evening you rely on the Buddha's support.
Thus, on meeting danger, you pass beyond it.
When a benefactor shows you the way,
Resources and livelihood follow at that time.
Steady progress brings recognition in every direction. Renewing the old introduces no disaster. The image is unseen divine support: patience is traditionally highly favorable.

In Journey to the West, the pilgrims approach the sacred mountain and reach Lingyun Ferry. Xuanzang fears the single-log bridge. A sacred boatman offers a bottomless boat; after falling into the river and being lifted out, Xuanzang sees his mortal body drift away. The episode represents passing beyond the mortal condition on the way to receiving the scriptures.
Nüwa Smelts Stones
Once, while sailing, you lost a needle.
Today you still search the sea for it.
Even if the original needle could be found,
It would cost both effort and anxious thought.

Blessing is the foundation of livelihood, and livelihood the seed of blessing. The teaching is made plain: remain especially cautious. The image is searching the sea for a needle: matters cost great effort and care.
The Chinese edition supplies only the allusion's title, Nüwa Smelts Stones, without a narrative. No additional story has been inserted into this translation.
Water Spilled Before the Horse
A fish swims within the blue-green pond.
Suddenly a net closes in on every side.
It thinks and thinks, but finds no way to turn and escape.
In the end the matter brings further trouble.
While one rests beneath a roof, misfortune falls from above. Recognize it early and take precautions. The image is a fish caught in a net: vigilance is needed.

The poor woodcutter and scholar Zhu Maichen is abandoned by his wife, who remarries. Later he gains office as governor of Kuaiji. She asks to return, even as a servant. He pours out a bucket of water and says reunion is possible only if it can be gathered again. He gives the couple land to farm, but the tale ends with her death by drowning and his payment for her burial.
Sun Bin Traps Pang Juan
The joy before your eyes is not yet true joy.
Even without immediate peril, there is no real peace.
Why cut your own flesh to patch a wound?
Better keep to established ways and await the time.
Stop when you know you should; let the heart relax when it can. Cutting your own flesh only creates another pain. The image is wounding oneself: remain with established ways and wait.

Sun Bin and Pang Juan study together, but Pang envies Sun's ability and has him mutilated. Sun escapes by feigning madness and becomes strategist in Qi. He lures Pang by reducing visible cooking fires, then sets an ambush at Maling. Unlike lot 10's account, this version says Pang realizes escape is impossible and kills himself beneath a tree.
The Overlord Is Surrounded
The road is dangerous, the horse weary, and the traveler hurried.
Soldiers separated from their company are equally distressed.
At the rapids, wind and waves break the boat's oars.
As day fades and flowers wither, frost descends.
Keep to established ways and wait; quiet brings no blame. Do not strain after schemes, but remain at ease. The image is a broken boat descending rapids: guard against danger and obstruction.

Xiang Yu, Overlord of Chu, believes his army invincible. Han Xin and the allied lords surround him at Gaixia in the traditional account. As morale collapses, Xiang breaks out and reaches the Wu River. Though a boat can carry him across, he feels unable to face the people of Jiangdong after his defeat and takes his own life.
A Gold Spirit Tests Dou Yi
A golden balance weighs your heart.
Nothing is added or subtracted; neither side is heavier.
Throughout life, keep your heart upright.
Learning is complete, and skill shines clearly.
An even, upright heart brings lasting peace. Fulfill your proper responsibilities and all is tranquil. The image is fairness and integrity: steadiness without ill fortune.

After Dou Yanshan's good deeds, his five sons become distinguished. One son, Dou Yi, lodges at an inn. Heaven sends a gold spirit disguised as a neighboring girl to test him. He refuses her entry despite threats of self-harm and finally pursues her with a sword. She becomes golden light and vanishes into the ground, where he finds a gold ingot.
Celebrating the Prince of Fenyang's Birthday
The household is filled with exceptional celebration.
A family that accumulates goodness flourishes.
Marriage, fields, and silkworms all accord with hopes.
Illness meets a fitting remedy and finds relief.
A household that cultivates goodness has blessings to spare. Loyalty and righteousness stand beneath a fortunate star. The image is a household in celebration: affairs proceed smoothly.

Guo Ziyi, Prince of Fenyang, is honored for his Tang military service, steady strategy, and fair command. His birthday gathers family and friends in joyful celebration. In the tale, seven sons and eight sons-in-law all hold high office. Their ceremonial tablets pile up across a bed, symbolizing the family's prosperity, distinction, and longevity.
The Plum Blossoms a Second Time
Winter brings a plum tree upon the ridge.
Its leaves fall and branches dry, but it is not destroyed.
Let the warming spring arrive swiftly.
Once more it takes first place among the flowers.
An arrow seems to miss its mark, yet the effort is not wholly empty. Wait for spring: distinction lies within it. The image is the plum taking first place; delay is traditionally favorable.

After Mei Kui is killed, his rescued son Mei Liangyu lives under the name Wang Xitong with Chen Risheng, his father's friend. Blossoming plums prompt a memorial offering, but a storm strips them bare. Chen, his daughter Xingyuan, and Liangyu pray for another flowering, which the legend grants. Liangyu later wins first place in the examinations and marries Xingyuan.
Li Mi Rebels Against Tang
Day after day you are like a bee gathering flowers.
You fly to the southwest and then hurry east.
Spring ends; the blossoms fade, leaving nowhere to seek them.
Yet your heart will not change its former course.
Spring's beauty cannot be found; long rain does not clear. In planning and enterprise, stillness is preferable. The image is a bee gathering flowers: toil and anxious effort.

At the end of Sui, Li Mi leads the Wagang forces and calls himself King of Wei. His generals gradually join Li Yuan's Tang cause. Li Mi and Wang Bodang eventually join as well. This edition adds a marriage to a princess before Li Mi rebels, kills his wife, and dies under a volley of arrows at thirty-seven. These details are presented as the source's story.
Wenjun Visits Xiangru
You recognize the azure dragon descending to the busy streets.
That year a woman marries a second husband.
It is like setting two arrows upon one bow.
One fears the dragon-horse will find no settled home.

Repeated complications cannot be escaped. The commentary attributes matters to heaven's decree and urges careful restraint. The image is two arrows on one bow; it nevertheless regards renewed union as favorable.

The widowed Zhuo Wenjun loves literature and hears Sima Xiangru play the qin. They meet at night, discover mutual affection, and elope to Chengdu. Poor, they return to Linqiong and sell wine together. Xiangru is later recognized by Emperor Wu and takes office. The source glosses jiuqu as a bustling city street.
Wang Mang Recruits the Worthy
You keep bees because you seek their honey.
Yet beware the sting upon their tails.
The road before your eyes takes an unexpected turn.
In secret it runs deep through a forest of thorns.
Examine matters carefully and do not force them. What justifies taking honey from bees? The image combines labor with the risk of gaining bitterness while seeking sweetness; guard against calamity.

Wang Mang benefits from his aunt's position as Empress Yuan. He cultivates modest conduct, generosity, and ties with able men. He later usurps Han and founds Xin. The source says his restoration of ancient institutions worsens suffering, and links Liu Xiu's subsequent rise with the restoration of Eastern Han.
The Chenqiao Coup
Spring thunder sounds, and countless insects stir and call.
With one turn they rise out of the mud.
Only then is movement back and forth understood.
A single morning's transformation makes a dragon.
Thunder signals a turn of time; going out and returning both have their place. A sudden change reaches heaven's gate. The image is thunder awakening insects: meeting a benefactor is favorable.

Zhao Kuangyin serves as commander under Later Zhou. After Emperor Shizong dies, a child succeeds him. On campaign at Chenqiao, the troops urge Zhao to rule. They place a yellow robe upon him as he lies intoxicated, then return to the capital and replace the child emperor. The source notes that coup describes the event more aptly than voluntary abdication.
Qin Is Defeated and Three Commanders Are Captured
Like a swan, you fly straight into a cage.
You wish to turn back, but find no passage.
North, south, east, and west offer no way out.
This lot fears regret without end.
Advancement is impossible, retreat difficult. Lower your head and face what lies within the situation. The image is a bird entering a cage: much appearance and little substance.

Duke Mu of Qin ignores an elder minister's warning and sends troops toward Zheng. Jin lures Qin's army into a dangerous valley, blocks the way ahead, attacks from both sides with fire, and closes in from behind. Qin's soldiers trample one another amid heavy losses, and all three commanders are captured.
Wu Yuan Leaves Zhaoguan by Night
It is like carrying a tiger across a high mountain.
You tremble with fear, your courage chilled.
Before you notice, a favorable turn may come.
Even so, take care to preserve your own safety.
Danger upon danger obstructs the road ahead. Any undertaking involves hardship. The image is carrying a tiger over a mountain: peril and alarm accompany affairs.

Wu Yuan, known as Wu Zixu, flees pursuit by King Ping of Chu, hiding by day and traveling by night. At Zhaoguan, the border guards fail to recognize him because worry has turned his hair white overnight. He passes safely into Wu. The overnight transformation belongs to the legend.
The Hongwu Emperor Herds Cattle
Fish and dragons mingle, sharing the same intention.
Patiently remain in the deep pool until fortune opens.
One morning, unexpectedly, the head rises above the water.
A leap through Yu's Gate reaches the dragon palace.

Although foundations are growing, the time must still be awaited. Build undertakings from their proper basis and avoid rash action. The image is fish and dragons before transformation: await the right moment.

Zhu Yuanzhang, later the Hongwu Emperor and founder of Ming, grows up poor and herds cattle for a landowner. The source uses his humble beginning as the image of a dragon concealed in a deep pool, awaiting the time to rise.
Returning the Jade Intact to Zhao
In a dream you speak of possessing great wealth.
Reputation beyond the clouds arrives without substance.
Across distant mountains and waters, reports are hard to trust.
A benefactor's guidance brings a smile.
Like recounting a dream within a dream, reputation is not to be relied upon. Await a favorable time and guidance. The image is dream treasure: much appearance and little substance.

The powerful Qin offers fifteen cities for Zhao's He jade. Lin Xiangru takes the jade to Qin but sees that the ruler means to keep it without paying. He threatens to smash it rather than allow this. By his resourcefulness, the jade ultimately returns intact to Zhao. The episode is the source of the well-known expression.
Rescuing the Ruler at Lintong
Cold water, not yet heated, is a pale broth.
Neither cold nor hot, it holds a gentle warmth.
To travel the world without further trouble,
Rely on the many strong skills within yourself.

A prisoner meets pardon; illness meets a good physician. A benefactor guides the pursuit of livelihood and other hopes. The image is proceeding in a balanced, ordinary way: stability is highly favorable.

Late in Sui, Li Yuan passes beneath Mount Lintong. Qin Qiong, also called Shubao, is sleeping in a temple to Wu Yuan when cries awaken him. He breaks through the encirclement, drives off the attackers, and saves Li Yuan's family. The tale connects this rescue with Qin's later service as a founding Tang general.
Secret Help Overthrows the Bronze Banner
In empty uncertainty you make a vow for safety.
Once safe, you leave the vow unfulfilled.
Do not forget the sacred pledge: fulfill it.
Know this divine reminder, and do not treat it lightly.
People have their own views; there is no need for anxious haste. Do not slight Guanyin's instruction. The image favors what is trustworthy over what is empty and counsels constancy.

At Dongling Pass, Yang Yicheng sets the Bronze Banner formation, which Qin Shubao cannot defeat. Qin learns that the defending officer Luo Cheng is his cousin and contacts Luo's mother. She directs her son to support the formation openly while secretly helping Qin. Qin breaks the formation and captures the pass.
Zhiyuan Joins the Army
You climb straight to the immortal's crag to learn the Way.
Who knew that one day the emperor would summon you?
The sun and moon keep shining in the blue sky.
An upright heart carries a good name throughout the world.

Carry matters through from beginning to end; do not turn aimlessly east and west. Act with a settled purpose and many benefactors appear. The image is being guided by helpful people: harmony is highly favorable.

Liu Zhiyuan, also written Liu Zhiyuan with a different character, lives in poverty with his wife Li Sanniang. An uncle sends him to a melon garden hoping spirits will devour him. In the legend he defeats them, finds a sword, leaves his wife to enlist, and rises in office. After the Khitan destroy Jin, he proclaims Later Han at Jinyang.
A Favorable Wind Carries Wang Bo to Tengwang Pavilion
The parasol tree sheds its leaves as autumn nears its end.
The traveler hastens home like a passing cloud.
Thanks to heaven's vigorous assistance,
A favorable wind brings the boat home laden with treasures.
Heaven accords with the undertaking held in the heart; plans may be carried out. The image is falling parasol-tree leaves, with adversity preceding good fortune.

Wang Bo longs to attend the rebuilt Tengwang Pavilion at Nanchang. A water deity promises him a favorable wind in a dream. He wakes, finds a boat, and swiftly covers the great distance, then writes the famous Preface to Tengwang Pavilion. The source includes a verse connecting his poetic gift and later immortality with the deity's aid. Its stated reign date conflicts with Wang Bo's lifetime.
Fire in Gourd Valley
Blazing flames stretch upward to the sky.
Yet within the fire a lotus blooms.
In the end it comes to fulfillment without injury.
Leaves still grow, with roots and branches intact.

Although danger is encountered, the person remains unharmed. Benefactors appear in undertakings. The image is a lotus growing in fire: apparent danger does not become actual injury in the traditional reading.

Following defeat at Red Cliffs, Cao Cao flees through ambushes arranged by Kongming. Resting at Gourd Valley, he laughs that such dangerous ground has no ambush. Then a signal sounds, Zhang Fei attacks, and fire spreads through the valley. Cao escapes in disorder toward Huarong Road.
Li Yuan Takes the Throne
It is like the moon on the third, fourth, or fifth night.
Part absent, part present, it is not yet whole.
Wait for the fair night of the fifteenth.
Then light and fullness reach everywhere.
Keep to established ways and await the time, like a newly risen moon. Wait for fullness and the outlook becomes favorable. The image is the moon not yet full: timing brings good fortune.

The source links Li Yuan's accession in 618 with news of Emperor Yang of Sui's death. He establishes Tang and rules for nine years before Li Shimin succeeds him. The tale symbolizes circumstances improving gradually. Its placement of the accession at Taiyuan is a historical inaccuracy in the Chinese source.
Zhuangzi Tests His Wife
What comes of losing virtue for the sake of reputation?
Beware lest good fortune change into misfortune.
Drunk with wine, you no longer know where you go.
Beneath the pines' shadows, the dream remains dim.
A fish leaves water in the cold: something is lacking within apparent perfection. Better not initiate a new undertaking. The image is a fish out of water, and the commentary urges against movement.

In this popular story, Zhuangzi feigns death to test his wife and expose the changeability of human attachment. The source reads it as a warning that hidden trouble may lie within an apparently complete situation, and that one's own wishes should not be mistaken for reality.
Han Wengong Encounters Snow
Clouds open and mist covers the road before the mountain.
Amid the world's cycles, the moon becomes full again.
If poetry and learning wake you from a deep dream,
A benefactor guides your steps toward Tiantai.
An older person pursues a hope; flowers reopen at spring's end. Fame and benefit are sought, and unexpected gain arrives late. The image is flowers blooming after spring: change comes later.

Han Yu, courtesy name Tuizhi and posthumously Wengong, protests the reception of a Buddha relic and is demoted to Chaozhou. Snow blocks his horse at Blue Pass. He then understands a verse earlier attributed to his nephew Han Xiangzi: clouds cross the Qinling Mountains; snow fills Blue Pass. The tale ends with Han donating his possessions and becoming an immortal; that ending is legendary.
Shang Lu Wins First Place Three Times
Spring flowers open and shine upon the sunlit terrace.
From ten thousand miles away, carts bring precious wealth.
If you pass the three tiers of waves at Yu's Gate,
It is like thunder suddenly sounding over level ground.

Receiving office at court is like a poor person finding treasure. Plans accord with the heart; the commentary ranks this among the finest images. Appearing before the emperor signifies great traditional good fortune.

Shang Lu of Ming wins first place successively in the provincial, metropolitan, and palace examinations, becoming jieyuan, huiyuan, and zhuangyuan. The source presents this triple distinction as an example of an ambition fulfilled at a stroke.
Yaojin Explores the Underground Cavern
Halfway up the ridge, the traveler sees the sun touch the mountain.
Steep slopes and rocky cliffs offer no safe rest.
Looking to heaven, you ask for protection.
Even here, your person remains within the realm of peace.
Chisel stone to find jade; wash sand to find gold. Effort is needed and the heart is wearied. The image is finding gold amid danger, with the prospect of a benefactor.

At a feast celebrating military success, a deep chasm opens in the ground. Lots are drawn and Cheng Yaojin is chosen to explore it. Lowered on a rope, he finds stone doors, furniture, a bridge, and a table bearing an imperial robe and jade belt. He puts them on and emerges. The legend connects this with his three-year reign as the Demon King of Chaos.
Pang Hong Fears Judge Bao
A tiger made of wood stands before the gate.
It has an imposing appearance, but cannot hurt anyone.
It is plainly said that no harm is involved.
Yet worry and hesitation still alarm the heart.

Snow falls onto a hot stove; words pass like wind by the ear. Cultivate goodness: adversity comes first, good fortune later. The image is a wooden tiger's imposing appearance: much alarm and little substance.

Judge Bao governs Kaifeng under Song Emperor Renzong. Pang Hong, a powerful imperial relative, falsely imprisons General Di Qing. Alarmed when Bao requests the case, Pang tries to obstruct him. The truth exposes Pang's accusation as false. The emperor is asked to judge, but the source says Pang is released because of his royal connection.
Jiang Wei Is Won Over by Strategy
Going out and returning, your undertakings are highly favored.
It is like flawless jade hidden within a stone.
If a benefactor comes to guide you,
Then the treasure is found, bringing joy and distinction.
Jade lies within stone until a benefactor points it out. Finding it satisfies the heart. The image is treasure concealed in stone: fulfillment and great traditional good fortune.

Zhuge Liang admires Jiang Wei, a capable Wei officer devoted to his mother. In Romance of the Three Kingdoms, he attacks the city where she lives to draw Jiang away, while sending a disguised double to make Wei believe Jiang has defected. With no way back, Jiang surrenders. Zhuge receives him respectfully, and Jiang becomes sincerely loyal to Shu.
Weipei Encounters an Immortal
Suddenly a message is said to fly toward heaven.
A boat returns full of treasures from Mount Tai.
If you ask whether the journey will bring good things,
Ahead, a benefactor is still helping you onward.

If you ask about achievement, a benefactor lies ahead. Joy increases, and livelihood and resources are abundant. The image is accomplishment: advancement is highly favorable in the traditional reading.

The Chinese edition tells of a recluse surnamed Wei who meets an immortal in the mountains and receives instruction in the Way. It interprets the episode as inspiration accompanying good fortune and assistance from a benefactor. The given title's personal name is uncertain, so its spelling here follows the source rather than substituting another edition's story.
Three Heroes Fight Lü Bu
Unfurrow your troubled brow and step forward among the people.
The road ahead changes, bringing joy and resources.
A broad road opens, as wide as the sky.
In giving resources, let the heart be generous and at ease.
A broad road permits forward travel. Set your purpose upon what lies ahead. The image is an open and distinguished future: affairs are traditionally favorable.
The Three Kingdoms episode brings Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei together against Lü Bu. The source takes their combined effort as an image of working with one heart to overcome an opponent.
Cai Qing Repays Kindness
From youth you have traded, putting plans to use.
Livelihood and resources are abundant without insistent seeking.
If two people undertake a shared purpose,
A scholar goes out and returns as the top examination graduate.
From childhood to maturity, the way is unobstructed. Deliberate enterprise and achievement proceed smoothly. The image is trading from youth: diligence and thrift remove anxiety.

The source identifies Cai Qing with Cai Bojie, also called Cai Yong, in a dramatic tale. While he goes to the capital for examinations, his impoverished wife Zhao Wuniang survives on coarse food with help from their neighbor Zhang Guangcai. After winning first place, Cai returns and learns of the assistance. Husband and wife visit Zhang to offer thanks and a gift of silver.
Gao Junbao's Marriage
The luan and phoenix have their feathers drenched by rain.
For the moment, even sparrows bully them.
One day the clouds will finally open.
Then their fine plumage will be restored as before.
The petty gain strength; the upright should not compete with them. Keep to your proper course and act when the time comes. The image is a rain-soaked phoenix: waiting brings greater advantage.

Gao Junbao, son of Gao Huaide, leads two hundred soldiers with supplies to rescue Zhao Kuangyin during a campaign against Southern Tang. At Double-Lock Mountain, the female outlaw Liu Jinding captures him and insists on marriage. The couple then lead their followers through the encirclement to rescue Zhao.
Boya Visits His Friend
An upright person should not imitate petty conduct.
If affairs go wrong, each side makes accusations.
The qin must be heard by someone who understands its music.
Keep to your steady course in quiet, and some clarity may come.
Only a true understanding friend can appreciate you. Leave idle affairs alone; wait for a benefactor and joy follows. The image is meeting a kindred spirit: constancy is favorable.

The qin player Boya meets the woodcutter Zhong Ziqi, who understands his music. They become sworn friends and agree to meet again a year later. Boya returns to find Ziqi dead. At his grave, Boya breaks his strings and shatters the qin, asking for whom he could play now that his understanding listener is gone. The tale contrasts plentiful acquaintances with the rarity of a true confidant.
Cao Pi Proclaims Himself Emperor
Ambition and achievement call for effort day by day.
For now, wine and sensual pleasure are indulged to excess.
If the golden rooster brings its message to you,
Wealth, blessings, and emoluments are summoned to your side.

Ambition stirs the heart; it is not too late to keep your proper course. The golden rooster announces its promise, bringing joy. The image is aspiration to distinction: constancy is highly favorable in the traditional commentary.

Cao Pi, Cao Cao's second son, replaces Emperor Xian of Han and establishes Wei. The source then incorrectly says that Sima Yan deposes Cao Pi seven years later. Historically Sima Yan replaces the later Wei emperor Cao Huan in 265. This note preserves the source's subject while identifying that conflation.
Dou Yanshan Accumulates Good Deeds
The lofty jeweled pagoda is no ordinary sight.
Its eight clear sides radiate light.
I urge you to set your resolve and bow with devotion.
Through good deeds, heaven bestows blessings.

These blessings are visible to all; there is no need for anxious haste. The commentary attributes them to previously established merit. The image is virtue becoming manifest: affairs are traditionally highly auspicious.

Dou Yanshan reaches middle age without a son. His father appears in a dream and tells him to abandon wrongdoing and practice goodness. Dou changes his conduct, helps others, and has five sons. The Three Character Classic praises his upright teaching and the distinction achieved by all five.
Six Expeditions Beyond Qishan
A candle lit in the wind casts only a thin, empty shadow.
Dimly, it seems to spread into flowers within a mirror.
Again and again, one tries to gather what appears there.
Who realizes it is only an illusory floating raft?

Wealth and rank are attributed to heaven, poverty to fate; the commentary treats both as predetermined. The image is lighting a candle in the wind: empty reputation offers no benefit. This describes the traditional text, not a factual claim about destiny.

In the Three Kingdoms tradition, Kongming repeatedly campaigns through Qishan against Wei without final success. The source associates the sixth expedition with his memorial on sending out the troops and his death at Wuzhang Plains. It uses the unfulfilled campaign to illustrate timing, fate, and effort that ends without its intended result; the sequence is the source's literary account.
Ji Ping Meets Disaster
Delay is advisable in setting out and pursuing plans.
Idle worry may provoke disputes.
Like a bird flying into a net,
How soon can one expect to escape confinement?

Maintain established ways and adapt to the time while awaiting a benefactor. Whatever the question, the central affair is delayed. The image is constancy amid circumstances: the traditional reading warns of frustration and ill fortune.

In the Three Kingdoms story, the physician Ji Ping resolves to kill Cao Cao because he controls the emperor. Called to treat a headache, Ji puts poison in the medicine. Cao discovers it and has him tortured. Ji denounces Cao and kills himself by striking his head against a stone pillar.
Tao Sanchun Takes Command
Rein in the horse, take up the whip, and come straight on.
Half is worry and peril, half calamity.
It is like a house consumed by fire.
Rain then descends from heaven, washing it into ashes.
A lifetime of toil: do not entangle yourself in disputes. When fetters arrive, resentment follows. The commentary calls this half sorrow and half joy and recommends good deeds in all matters.

Tao Sanchun, daughter of Tao Hong, marries Zheng En after a martial contest. Their son Zheng Yin marries Wang Yue'e, and all practice martial arts. Learning that Zheng En and Zhao Kuangyin are surrounded during a Southern Tang campaign, Tao leads her son and daughter-in-law to their aid. The two forces meet and return victorious.
The Three Teachings Discuss the Way
The insight of buddhas and deities is made known to you.
A deluded person's talk only deepens confusion.
An elder obtains the sacred lot and departs.
Better maintain established ways and wait for the time to come.
The complete set of sacred lots has now spoken. Keep your existing position and wait for the proper time. The image is constancy without movement: waiting is favorable in the traditional reading.

Representatives of Buddhism, Daoism, and Confucianism discuss truth together. The source treats this final lot as a return to one's own heart, emphasizing cultivation of character and virtue as the closing message of the collection.
